summary: The narrator, alone in the rain at the Mayan site of Baalum, sees a bleached jaguar skin hung beside a paved pathway and mistakes it for a lurking threat before realizing it is a dead cat. He heads across the plaza to climb a steep, newly restored pyramid, where he finds a stone hut with a roof at the top. Reflecting on the site, he compares its reconstruction to Sir Arthur Evans's reconstruction of the Palace of Minos on Crete, wondering whether the pyramid is a fake or the obsession of someone crazed. The passage is fearful and atmospheric, and it references the earlier death of Sarah and a suspected attacker named Ramos.
one_line: Alone at the Mayan ruin of Baalum in a storm, the narrator meets a bleached jaguar skin, then climbs a restored pyramid and questions whether it is authentic.
key_facts: The narrator sighted a white form at the south, forested edge of the plaza and ducked down, fearing it was someone lurking to beat him to death as they had Sarah.
The narrator wondered whether Ramos intended to murder him immediately.
The narrator's yellow plastic flashlight beam was swallowed up in the rain.
The white form was the skin of a jaguar, bleached white, with the head still on and fearsome teeth bared, hung beside the paved pathway.
The narrator described his first encounter at Baalum as being with a spooky, dead cat.
The narrator headed toward a pyramid that was barely visible in the rain.
The steps of the pyramid were steeper than the narrator had thought but appeared to be part of meticulous restoration and brand-new.
A stone hut with what appeared to be a roof stood at the top of the pyramid.
Sir Arthur Evans, an eccentric Brit archaeologist, reconstructed the Palace of Minos on Crete with his own money about a hundred years earlier.
The Palace of Minos on Crete is still a tourist highlight, according to the narrator.
The narrator asked why somebody could not do the same with a reclaimed Mayan pyramid in Central America.
The narrator felt the pyramid had the feel of being somebody's crazed obsession, unlike the Minos reconstruction.
The building crowning the pyramid was also a restoration, including a decorated wooden lintel above the door that looked newly made.
The narrator described the night songs of the birds as ominous, with the primeval forest reasserting its will.
